prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Imagine that Alice and Bob, who have never met and share no password, want to agree on a secret number while Eve, a stranger, writes down every word they say to each other, and consider first how this could possibly work, because on the face of it the task looks impossible: anything Alice tells Bob, Eve hears too, so whatever Bob needs in order to reach the secret, Eve seems to have as well. The way out is that some calculations are easy to do in one direction and extremely tedious to undo, and public-key cryptography is the art of building a shared secret out of such one-way calculations, so that Alice and Bob each hold a private piece that never travels along the line and Eve is left holding only pieces that cannot be turned back into it.

A familiar picture is mixing paint. Suppose Alice and Bob publicly agree on a yellow paint that everyone, Eve included, can see. Alice privately picks a secret colour, say a particular red, mixes a generous amount of it into the yellow and sends the resulting orange across to Bob, while Bob does the same with his own secret blue and sends back a green. Mixing paint is easy but un-mixing it is practically impossible, since nobody can look at a bucket of orange and say exactly which red went in. Alice now takes Bob's green and stirs in her secret red, Bob takes Alice's orange and stirs in his secret blue, and both buckets end up containing yellow, red and blue in the same proportions, so both have the same muddy brown. Eve saw the yellow, the orange and the green, but to reach that brown she would need either Alice's red or Bob's blue, and neither was ever sent. The analogy has one flaw, which is that real paint can in practice be analysed by a clever chemist, so mathematicians needed an operation that cannot be unpicked even by a clever person with a very fast computer, and for that they borrowed something you have met at school, which is the arithmetic of a clock.

On a clock face, once you pass twelve you start again at one, so that ten hours after eight o'clock it is six, and mathematicians call this working modulo twelve. Nothing stops us using a clock with a different number of hours, and for the example here we will use one with 23 hours, writing "mod 23" to mean "take the remainder after dividing by 23". Alice and Bob agree in the open on two numbers, the clock size 23 and a base number 5, and everyone including Eve knows both. Now Alice secretly chooses the number 6, then multiplies 5 by itself six times and takes the remainder on the 23-hour clock. Doing the multiplication gives 15,625, and since 23 goes into that 679 times with 8 left over, Alice's public number is 8, which she sends to Bob. Bob secretly chooses 15, multiplies 5 by itself fifteen times and reduces the answer on the same clock, which gives 19, and he sends that to Alice. The numbers 8 and 19 travel openly, while 6 and 15 stay in the heads of their owners and never touch the line.

The finish is the part that feels like a conjuring trick. Alice takes Bob's number 19 and multiplies it by itself six times, using her secret 6, and after reducing on the 23-hour clock she gets 2. Bob takes Alice's number 8 and multiplies it by itself fifteen times, using his secret 15, and he also gets 2. They agree on 2 without ever sending it, and the reason is that each of them has in effect multiplied the base 5 by itself six times and fifteen times, in one order or the other, so that altogether it has been multiplied by itself ninety times. Since multiplying by itself six times and then fifteen times is the same as multiplying fifteen times and then six, the two routes meet at the same number whichever way round they are taken. Eve, who holds only 23, 5, 8 and 19, can reach 2 only if she can discover either 6 or 15, which means asking "what power of 5 gives 8 on this clock?" and answering it.

With a 23-hour clock Eve can answer that in a minute by trying 5, then 5 times 5, then the next power and so on until 8 appears, and this is why the real systems use clocks of astonishing size, numbers with six hundred or more digits, together with secrets of comparable length. Doing the forward step on such numbers is still quick for a computer, because there is a shortcut of repeated squaring that reaches a huge power in a few hundred steps instead of a few trillion trillion, whereas going backwards from the public number to the secret exponent has no known shortcut and the only general approach is trial and error, which with numbers of this size would outlast the lifetime of the universe on every computer ever built. The security therefore rests on a gap in effort, with the honest users paying a trivial price and the eavesdropper facing a cost beyond reach, and nobody has proved that no clever shortcut exists, only that nobody has found one after decades of serious attempts by people who would very much like to.

Everything so far has produced a shared number, and the usual next step is to use that number as the key for an ordinary fast scrambling method, one in which the same secret both locks and unlocks the message, so that the slow clock arithmetic is needed only once at the start of a conversation. There is also a second family of public-key methods, which is probably what people picture when they hear the phrase, in which each person owns a pair of linked numbers, one published to the world and one kept private. Anyone may use the published number to lock a message, but only the holder of the matching private number can unlock it, a bit like a padlock that you can snap shut without a key, leaving the only key in the hands of its owner. The most famous version relies on a different one-way task, the fact that multiplying two enormous prime numbers together takes a moment whereas starting from their product and recovering the two primes is hopelessly slow, and the same pairing, run the other way, lets a person prove that a message came from them, because only their private number could have produced a signature that the public number confirms.

One weakness deserves a mention, which is that Alice and Bob so far have no proof that the number they receive really comes from the person they think it does. If Eve could do more than listen, say by catching Alice's message and replying to her as though she were Bob while also talking to the real Bob as though she were Alice, she could agree one secret with each of them and quietly pass messages between the two while reading all of them. Defending against this needs some way of knowing that a public number truly belongs to its owner, which is why websites carry certificates signed by organisations your computer already trusts, and why the padlock in your browser stands for the two ideas working together, a shared secret made in public and a signature that ties it to the right party. The deepest point is that secrecy never had to be shared at the outset, since all that was ever shared was a way of making a secret that only the two ends of the conversation can finish.
